Reviewed sources and the chapter contract

This chapter teaches array representation, safe indexing and exact array transformations from first principles. It assumes that you can trace assignments, loops and function calls. The main language is C17. Explicitly marked comparisons use C0, Python 3 or C++. Mathematical algorithms use unbounded integers unless a machine range is specified. Numerical memory diagrams use a stated flat byte-address model; they do not authorize otherwise invalid C pointer operations.

Four primary written courses contribute different parts of the explanation: Cambridge Programming in C (Neel Krishnaswami, 2017–18), CMU 15-122 (Frank Pfenning and André Platzer, Fall 2026), Harvard CS50x (David J. Malan, 2025), and UC Berkeley CS61A / Composing Programs (John DeNero). Stanford CS106B (Chris Gregg, Fall 2016) is a fifth reviewed comparison for dynamic backing arrays. MIT 6.0001 (Ana Bell, Eric Grimson and John Guttag, Fall 2016) is a sixth reviewed comparison for list cloning and mutation during iteration. The source review records exact reading ranges, evaluated alternatives, selection criteria and corrections. References at the end link to written materials.

The central skill is to distinguish four things: a logical sequence, its allocated storage, the references that select that storage, and the sequence of writes that changes it. Address arithmetic alone cannot establish correctness. Every problem needs a domain, an access proof, a value relation and an explanation of whether the relation uses original or already modified values.

After reading, you should be able to derive row/column strides, invert a flat index, classify C array expressions, prove loop and copy invariants, detect alias corruption, calculate dynamic-array costs and explain Python shallow sharing. The worked bank emphasizes these mathematical and conceptual tasks. Two authentic examination items are explicitly labeled bridge revisits rather than newly discovered unique items. No finite source pool or test suite can guarantee all future examination questions.

Elements, boundaries and object representation

An abstract array of length n maps each integer index in 0≤i<n to one element. An array can repeat values; positions remain distinct even when values are equal. A segment A[l:r) contains indices l,l+1,…,r-1, requires 0≤l≤r≤n, and has length r-l. Its right boundary is not an element. The empty segment A[k:k) is valid for every boundary 0≤k≤n.

For a language with lower bound L and upper bound U, the length is U-L+1. The normalized index is i-L. A zero-length abstract sequence is useful, but a standard fixed C declaration cannot use a zero array bound. An empty logical sequence may instead have reserved capacity, or be represented by a pointer and length zero. A variable-length C array evaluated with a nonpositive bound is also invalid; do not turn a mathematical empty case into such a declaration.

A C array is a contiguous object consisting of elements of one element type. There is no extra gap between successive elements beyond what is included in each element's own size. An array of structures therefore uses the structure's full size, including any structure padding, as its stride. A pointer object stores a pointer value; it does not contain the whole pointed-to array. A Python list is a mutable sequence of object references and can contain heterogeneous objects. Its language contract does not promise the same raw layout as a C integer array.

Write the following initialization before doing any arithmetic:

int a[6] = {4, -2, 7};   /* Remaining elements are zero. */
int b[6];               /* Automatic elements are not initialized here. */
static int c[6];         /* Static-storage elements are zero-initialized. */

The first array has six elements, not three; the initializer leaves the final three equal to zero. Reading an uninitialized automatic integer element does not give a portable predictable value. An arbitrary external input array also needs an explicit validity and initialization assumption.

If the first element begins at byte address B and each element occupies w bytes, then the numerical storage model gives

addr(A[i])=B+w(i-L).

For A[-2:5] with inclusive declaration bounds, B=1200 and w=4, element 3 is at 1200+4(3+2)=1220. This example uses a language-independent declaration; ordinary C indices still start at zero. The array's final occupied byte is B+wn-1, while its one-past boundary is B+wn. Neither an arbitrary byte address nor a numerically aligned address proves that a live typed C object exists there.

Multidimensional layouts and inverse indices

A rectangular two-dimensional array with R rows and C columns has RC elements. Let row and column lower bounds be Lr,Lc, and normalize u=i-Lr, v=j-Lc. In row-major storage, all C entries of each earlier row precede the selected row, then v entries precede the selected column. Consequently,

orow=uC+v,addr(A[i,j])=B+w(uC+v).

In column-major storage, each earlier column contains R entries:

ocol=vR+u,addr(A[i,j])=B+w(vR+u).

These expressions count elements first and bytes second. For

R=3,C=4,w=8,B=2048

, index (2,1) has row-major offset 9 and address 2120; its column-major offset is 5 and address 2088. C's real rectangular array declaration uses row-major storage. Column-major here is a separate stated representation, not a switch in how C interprets its declared array.

The inverse follows from quotient and remainder. Given a valid row-major element offset 0≤o<RC, divide o by C: u=⌊o/C⌋ and v=omodC. For column-major, divide by R to recover v and u. For a byte address X, first check that X-B is nonnegative, divisible by w, and less than wRC. A byte inside an element is not necessarily that element's starting address.

For three normalized indices u,v,t in extents D1,D2,D3, row-major offset is

o=(uD2+v)D3+t=uD2D3+vD3+t.

This is mixed-radix notation. Its uniqueness follows by repeatedly taking remainder and quotient by the last extent. In d dimensions, the stride of axis k in row-major order is the product of all later extents. Changing one index by one changes the element offset by that stride. The same principle handles a general affine view with stated strides sk: o=∑k(ik-Lk)sk. Such a view may include gaps or reversed axes; it need not be a standalone C multidimensional array.

A true C declaration and an array of row pointers are different:

int grid[3][4];
int (*row)[4] = grid;  /* Pointer to a complete four-int row. */
int *rows[3];         /* Array of three int pointers: pointees need allocation. */

The first contains twelve integer objects. Its expression conversion gives a pointer to a row, so row + 1 advances by four integers. The last contains three pointer objects and makes no promise that the selected row allocations are adjacent, equally long or even valid. Casting grid to int ** cannot create the missing row-pointer objects. A numerical flattening formula also does not justify using pointer arithmetic beyond the first actual row subarray; for portable C, index grid[i][j] with valid row and column bounds.

Transposition of an R×C row-major logical matrix produces a C×R result. Original position (i,j) maps from iC+j to jR+i. A transpose view can swap strides without moving data; a copied transpose creates a different physical arrangement. Square in-place transposition swaps each pair i<j once and leaves the diagonal unchanged. Rectangular in-place transposition requires permutation cycles or extra storage and cannot use the square-only loop unchanged.

C arrays, pointers and legal accesses

In most expression contexts, a C array expression converts to a pointer to its first element. Important exceptions include an array operand of sizeof, an operand of unary &, and a string literal used to initialize an array. A real array's sizeof counts its full storage. A function parameter declared int a[] is adjusted to int *a, so sizeof a inside that function counts the pointer object. The function must receive an independent length or a stronger explicit contract.

int a[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10};
int *p = a + 2;
int x = p[-1];           /* Selects a[1], so x is 4. */
size_t n = sizeof a / sizeof a[0];  /* Five, in this actual-array scope. */

The subscript p[-1] does not mean “count from the end” as in Python. The identity p[k]=*(p+k) applies only when the resulting access is legal. Here p points at a[2], so -1 moves back to a[1]. For a pointer at a[r], permitted element-access offsets satisfy -r≤k<n-r. Pointer formation additionally permits k=n-r, the one-past position; dereferencing that position does not.

Pointer addition and subtraction must stay within one array object or its one-past boundary. Subtraction counts elements, not bytes, and its result must be representable in ptrdiff_t. The valid numerical byte difference is therefore not a justification for subtracting pointers into unrelated allocations. Relational comparisons between unrelated array pointers likewise cannot be used as a portable general address ordering.

Unary & applied to the complete array yields a pointer to the whole array type. a and &a can describe the same beginning of storage, but their types and increments differ: a + 1 advances one int after conversion; &a + 1 advances one five-int array. Equality of beginning locations is not equality of type or stride.

For an array with nonzero length, a + n is a legal one-past pointer useful as an exclusive end. A reverse loop using size_t must not rely on i >= 0 to stop, because size_t is unsigned. Use a boundary that decreases before the access:

for (size_t i = n; i > 0; ) {
    --i;
    use(a[i]);
}

The body runs n times and never computes n - 1 when n is zero. Check arithmetic used in allocation: before requesting n * sizeof *p bytes, establish

n≤⌊SIZE\_MAX/sizeof(*p)⌋

. A successful arithmetic check still needs successful allocation and a live valid object. realloc may move storage and invalidate earlier aliases; on failure the old allocation remains valid, so keep the old pointer until the result is known.

For a rectangular parameter, int a[][4] adjusts to int (*a)[4]. The column extent participates in the row stride. C variable-length parameter forms can express a run-time column count, with the relevant positive-bound and implementation-support conditions; int ** remains a different representation.

Traversals, reductions and proof obligations

Before tracing a loop, describe the exact visited indices. For increasing stride s>0 over the half-open segment [l,r), they are l+ts for nonnegative integers t with l+ts<r. The count is zero when l≥r; otherwise it is ⌈(r-l)/s⌉. For a reverse traversal starting at r-1 with decrement s, the count is the same. A separate stopping relation involving the destination index can prematurely terminate a copying procedure.

To sum a segment, define original values A0[k] and use the invariant

l≤i≤r,S=∑k=li-1A0[k].

Initially i=l and the empty sum is zero. The guard i<r together with the invariant proves a valid read. Adding the current value and advancing i extends the sum by exactly one term. At exit, i=r, so the required segment sum is obtained. The variant r-i decreases to zero. Machine integer addition separately needs representability of all partial sums.

Finding a minimum needs a nonempty input or an explicit optional-result convention. If the first element initializes the minimum, comparisons number n-1. If a mathematical positive-infinity sentinel initializes it, comparisons number n and the first value always causes an update. Strict comparison retains the first occurrence of a tied minimum; non-strict comparison retains the last. Do not assume independence when analyzing the random number of updates; the authentic PhD bridge below derives it with indicator expectations.

For prefix sums, reserve n+1 entries and define

P[0]=0,P[i+1]=P[i]+A[i],∑k=lr-1A[k]=P[r]-P[l].

The query formula follows by cancellation of the first l terms, and also works for an empty segment. A static array permits linear preprocessing and constant-time range-sum queries. A later element update invalidates every subsequent prefix value; do not claim unchanged query correctness after mutation.

The difference sequence satisfies D[0]=A[0] and D[i]=A[i]-A[i-1] for i>0. Adding c to A[l:r) changes only D[l] by +c and, if r < n, D[r] by -c. An n+1 boundary array can retain a right-end sentinel. Reconstruct by a prefix accumulation. This inverse relation explains range updates; it is not merely a pair of memorized signs.

For a two-dimensional prefix table indexed by boundaries, P has shape (R+1)×(C+1) and zero top/left edges. The recurrence and rectangle query are

P[i+1,j+1]=A[i,j]+P[i,j+1]+P[i+1,j]-P[i,j],
S=P[r2,c2]-P[r1,c2]-P[r2,c1]+P[r1,c1].

The final plus sign restores the overlap that the two subtractions removed twice. Half-open row and column bounds make empty rectangles and edge rectangles work without case-specific index subtraction. Native formulas below use a separate mathematical font.

Mutation order, copying and overlap

An in-place transformation reads the values currently stored, unless it explicitly snapshots the original input. For a=[1,2,3,4], the forward update a[i] += a[i-1] for i=1..3 produces [1,3,6,10], because each read uses a modified predecessor. Running the same statements in reverse produces [1,3,5,7], because the predecessor has not yet changed. Both are well-defined mathematical sequences of statements; they compute different maps.

For a copy between distinct arrays, let B receive A[l:r). After t iterations, the copy invariant states B[k]=A0[l+k] for 0≤k<t and 0≤t≤r-l. Destination index t and source index l+t are valid under the segment contract. The result array must have capacity at least r-l; a new allocation gives a distinct result even when the values match.

For a move within the same array from [s,s+m) to [d,d+m), original values are the desired specification. If d > s and the segments overlap, increasing-index copying overwrites source values that have not yet been read. Copy from the high end. If d < s, increasing-index copying is safe; decreasing-index copying may corrupt the source. If d=s, no change is required.

A rigorous reverse-copy invariant fixes the already copied suffix to original values and states that the remaining source prefix is unmodified. At step t descending from m-1, destination d+t lies above source s+t, so it cannot overwrite any still unread smaller source index. This is the reason for the direction, not a convention to memorize.

For disjoint arrays, source and destination are different objects. For a C move within one known backing array, compare integer offsets to select the direction. Do not compare unrelated pointers with > as a general portable overlap test. The library memmove supports valid overlapping byte regions using an as-if temporary-copy contract. memcpy requires nonoverlap. A language-level element-copy loop is more appropriate for object types whose semantics are not simply raw byte copying.

The reviewed CMU copying proof omits an important alias restriction: its postcondition compares final source and final target segments. When overlapping writes modify the source, even the asserted copied-prefix relation can fail. This chapter uses original-input snapshots in its specification and either disjointness or an overlap-safe move. The correction is demonstrated in both the problem bank and an animation.

A complete overlap-safe element implementation

The following function moves elements within one known integer array. Its caller supplies a live initialized backing array with n elements whenever a nonempty move is requested. The function validates offsets before subtraction, so its tests do not themselves overflow. A zero-length move performs no pointer arithmetic or access and may use a null backing pointer. No unrelated-pointer ordering is needed.

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

bool move_ints(int *a, size_t n, size_t s, size_t d, size_t m) {
    if (s > n || d > n) return false;
    if (m > n - s || m > n - d) return false;
    if (m == 0 || s == d) return true;
    if (d > s) {
        size_t k = m;
        while (k > 0) {
            --k;
            a[d + k] = a[s + k];
        }
    } else {
        for (size_t k = 0; k < m; ++k)
            a[d + k] = a[s + k];
    }
    return true;
}

For the descending branch, at boundary k the target suffix with relative indices k through m−1 equals the corresponding original source suffix. The original source prefix with relative indices below k remains unchanged. After decrement, the read occurs at s+k and the write at d+k. Since d>s, the write is strictly above that source position and therefore above every remaining unread source position. The access checks give s+k<n and d+k<n without requiring an unchecked sum s+m. At k=0, the target is the entire original segment. The ascending branch has the dual invariant: the completed target prefix is correct, and the unread source suffix remains original because d<s. Both branches decrease their number of unprocessed elements by one. For a disjoint rightward move, descending order remains correct even though forward order would also work.

These validations establish ranges, not allocation authenticity: a caller that lies about n or supplies an expired pointer violates the backing-object contract. Returning true means the stated move was performed under that contract; it cannot prove facts about memory that C does not expose as metadata.

To insert at index k in a logical sequence of length n with spare capacity, move original positions n-1 down to k into positions n down to k+1, then write the new element and increase the length. There are n-k shifts. Deletion at k uses forward moves from k+1 through n-1 and decreases the length, for n-k-1 shifts. Old bytes outside the shortened logical prefix need not vanish; capacity and logical length are different.

Reversal swaps (l+t,r-1-t) for 0≤t<⌊(r-l)/2⌋. Its invariant fixes both completed ends and preserves the original untouched middle. Three reversals rotate a nonempty sequence left by k: reverse [0:k), reverse [k:n), then reverse [0:n). Normalizing k modulo n requires n>0; handle the empty sequence before that division. A cycle method uses gcd(n,k) cycles and visits every index exactly once.

The boundary form below avoids unsigned n−1 when the segment is empty. The caller validates l≤r≤n and the backing array before entry. In each iteration r−l>1 guarantees two distinct live indices after decrementing r. An odd middle entry is left alone; there are exactly floor((r−l)/2) pair swaps relative to the original segment length.

void reverse_segment(int *a, size_t l, size_t r) {
    while (r - l > 1) {
        --r;
        int saved = a[l];
        a[l] = a[r];
        a[r] = saved;
        ++l;
    }
}

Python slices, sharing and nested rows

Python single indexing normalizes a negative integer i to n+i and then requires a valid element. Slicing instead normalizes and clips boundaries, then follows a nonzero step. Positive steps default to start zero and stop n; negative steps default to start n-1 and a special before-first stop. The special omitted stop is different from an explicit -1, which normalizes to the last index. Consequently a[::-1] reverses a sequence, while a[:-1:-1] is empty.

After normalization, positive-step selected indices are a+ts<b and negative-step selected indices are a+ts>b. Counting them gives a ceiling divided by the step magnitude when the respective interval is nonempty. Use slice(...).indices(n) when auditing Python's exact boundary normalization. A zero step raises ValueError; an out-of-range single index raises IndexError, while a clipped ordinary slice can simply be empty.

a = [[2], [5]]
b = a[:]             # New outer list, same inner lists.
b[0].append(7)       # Also visible through a[0].
b[1] = [9]           # Rebinds only b's second slot.

After the first mutation, both outer lists contain a first reference to [2,7]. After the second, a is [[2,7],[5]] and b is [[2,7],[9]]. A shallow copy does not copy recursively referenced objects. A row comprehension that creates a fresh row each time avoids the repeated-row problem:

bad = [[0] * 3] * 2
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
bad[0][1] = 8         # Both displayed rows change.
good[0][1] = 8        # Only the first row changes.

An ordinary step-one slice assignment can change the list's length. An extended slice with a step other than one requires exactly as many replacement items as selected slots. Mutating a list while iterating can skip shifted elements: the iterator advances its position while deletion moves the next element left. A safe filtering construction makes a new output or uses a carefully proved read/write compaction loop.

Python string elements are Unicode code points, whereas C char-array bytes and UTF-8 encoding lengths describe different units. One displayed grapheme may contain several code points. Reversal by code points is not automatically a correct visual reversal of human text. These distinctions prevent importing a byte-address formula into Python string indexing.

C strings, terminators and bounded searching

A C string is a sequence of character values ending at its first zero character within accessible storage. Capacity, initialized bytes and string length are separate quantities. char s[] = "cat" allocates four characters; strlen(s) is three and sizeof s is four in that actual-array scope. char t[3] = "cat" is allowed in C but lacks the terminator, so it is not a valid string for strlen or %s. An embedded zero ends the string earlier even if later bytes remain in the array.

The string literal used through const char *p = "cat" must not be modified. A writable array initialized from the literal can be modified within its bounds. p's sizeof measures the pointer. strlen requires a terminator and scans up to it; the return type is size_t, not int. The final zero is a real array element, unlike the one-past pointer.

Searching m pattern characters in a text of length n requires candidate starts 0≤s≤n-m when m≤n. Each comparison reads text[s+t] with 0≤t<m, hence s+t<n. In the worst case, a direct search performs (n-m+1)m character comparisons, but successful early matches and mismatches can reduce that count. For m=0, specify a match at the starting boundary. For m>n, return failure before subtracting unsigned lengths.

def first_match(text, pattern):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0:
        return 0
    if m > n:
        return -1
    for start in range(n - m + 1):
        j = 0
        while j < m and text[start + j] == pattern[j]:
            j += 1
        if j == m:
            return start
    return -1

This code is a complete bounded-search model, not a C library replacement. Returning a C pointer into a caller-owned text additionally depends on that text's lifetime. Command-line argv is an array of pointers to strings, with argv[argc] null; that final pointer is different from each argument's final zero character. If argc is zero, argv[0] is the null sentinel and cannot be read as a program-name string.

Character conversion using a numeric difference assumes an encoding such as ASCII. C's ctype operations accept EOF or an unsigned-char-representable value; a negative signed char must first be converted to unsigned char. Do not assume that bytewise uppercase conversion handles arbitrary UTF-8 text.

Capacity growth and exact operation costs

A dynamic array maintains 0≤n≤c, where n is logical length and c is allocated capacity. Its occupied logical prefix is [0:n); allocated spare slots are [n:c). Insertion requires free capacity or expansion. Expansion allocates a new backing block, copies the n live elements, changes the owning reference and releases the old block under the appropriate ownership rules. Any earlier interior pointer into released storage becomes invalid.

Under the simple doubling model with initial capacity 1, successful appends allocate capacities 1,2,4,8,... . Copy work through a final capacity c is

1+2+4+…+c2=c-1.

For n≥1, the smallest power-of-two c at least n satisfies n≤c<2n. Hence copied elements are less than 2n and total writes including the n new elements are less than 3n. This proves amortized constant append cost under unit-cost element copying, while one expansion append still has linear cost. It does not say that every individual append is constant-time.

Doubling is not uniquely optimal. A fixed factor g>1 also produces a geometric total; its time/space constants differ. An additive increment instead creates quadratic total copying when it is fixed as n grows. Allocation time, element-copy behavior, cache effects and peak memory are outside the simplest unit-copy model and must be stated if included.

When c live elements expand to 2c, both blocks can coexist during copying, so the peak backing capacity is 3c slots. The final capacity alone misses that peak. A container with owned nested allocations also requires correct copy/move semantics; copying pointer values alone may produce shared ownership bugs. Shrinking at exactly half-full can repeatedly grow/shrink under alternating operations. A separate lower shrink threshold supplies hysteresis.

Two-dimensional traversal order affects a stated locality model. For a row-major matrix, visiting successive columns in one row accesses adjacent elements. Visiting one column down the rows uses a stride of C elements. Arithmetic operation counts may be equal while cache-line accesses differ. A precise cache question must state line size, alignment, cache capacity, replacement assumptions and reuse; “row-major is always faster” is not a theorem.

Packed representations and advanced index reasoning

For a lower-triangular n×n matrix storing its diagonal in row order, valid normalized indices satisfy 0≤j≤i<n. Earlier row lengths are 1 through i, so

o=i(i+1)2+j,N=n(n+1)2.

For an upper triangle in row order, row i has n-i entries and earlier rows contain in-i(i-1)/2 entries:

o=in-i(i-1)2+(j-i),0≤i≤j<n.

These are representation-dependent formulas. For a symmetric matrix stored only in its lower triangle, replace (i,j) by

(max(i,j),min(i,j))

before applying the lower formula. Multiplication and division must be ordered or widened so that a finite implementation does not overflow its intermediate product. The final representability of a triangular count does not alone ensure that i(i+1) fits.

A jagged matrix with row lengths r0,…,rR-1 can be packed into one flat sequence using boundary offsets Q[0]=0 and Q[i+1]=Q[i]+ri. Element (i,j) lies at Q[i]+j for 0≤j<ri. Repeated offsets represent empty rows. Recovering a row from a flat position must locate a nonempty interval containing it, rather than taking the first equal boundary blindly.

A circular buffer with positive capacity c maps logical offset t from head h to (h+t)modc. Maintain the length separately to distinguish empty from full when head equals tail. For negative integer rotations, normalize with mathematical modulo in [0:c); C's signed remainder may be negative and requires an explicit correction. The empty-capacity case cannot use modulo at all.

An in-place read/write compaction has invariant 0≤w≤r≤n, with A[0:w) equal to the retained original values from A[0:r) in their original order. Because w never exceeds r, writing A[w] cannot damage unread positions above r. This gives a stable filter with linear reads and at most n writes. It is a proof about dependency direction, closely related to safe leftward copying.

Question 1. Recursive reverse-stride copying

Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation

MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a, starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0). Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure.

1.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

2.

if(n<i)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

3.

if(n<i)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+1);

4.

if(n<0)return; b[i++]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+2);

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 1.

  1. After t calls, the intended state is n=N-1-2t and i=t. Thus the next recursive call must decrease the source index by two and increase the destination by one.
  2. Option 1 preserves this state and stops precisely when the source index becomes negative. It writes ⌈N/2⌉ elements.
  3. Option 2 leaves b[0] unwritten and stops too early through an unrelated comparison. Option 3 uses stride one. Option 4 also uses source stride one and has incompatible destination updates.
  4. The source lists pseudocode resembling C without parameter type declarations; it is not a strictly compilable C17 function. We assess its specified indexing algorithm, not missing declarations.

Transfer rule. Express the intended source and destination indices as functions of recursion depth.

Question 2. Expected running-minimum updates

Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation

Phd CS 1404 · Q72 · PDF page 16. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n, and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n?

1.

1

2.
lnn
3.

n

4.
nlnn
Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

  1. Let Ii indicate that position i contains the smallest of the first i values. Uniform permutation symmetry gives P(Ii=1)=1/i.
  2. Linearity of expectation requires no independence between these indicators: E[Y]=∑i=1n1/i=Hn.
  3. Integral bounds give ln(n+1)≤Hn≤1+lnn, so lnn is the listed large- n approximation.
  4. The exact mean is Hn, not exactly lnn. One counts only the first update; n assumes every position is a record; nlnn multiplies counts that should be summed.

Transfer rule. Distinguish the number of loop tests (always n) from the number of successful updates (random).

Original and course-inspired mathematical/conceptual problems

Question 3. A lower bound is not the first value

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A flat representation declares indices -3 through 8 inclusive, four-byte elements and base address 1600 for the first element. Find the address of index 5, total storage and final occupied byte.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

There are 8-(-3)+1=12 positions. Index 5 is eight positions after the first, regardless of the values stored. Its address is 1600+4(5+3)=1632. Storage is 12·4=48 bytes, so the last occupied byte is 1647 and the one-past boundary is 1648. Using 1600+4·5 would silently treat the lower bound as zero. The final byte and final element start differ by three. These are numerical layout statements; the negative declaration bound is not ordinary C array syntax.

Question 4. Invert a two-dimensional row-major address

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A matrix has row indices 2..6 and column indices -1..5. Each element occupies eight bytes; its first element starts at 4096. Which element starts at address 4312?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The byte difference is 216, divisible by eight, so the element offset is 27. There are seven columns. Divide 27=3·7+6: normalized row 3 and column 6 recover declared row 5 and column 5. Both lie in bounds. Thus the requested element is (5,5). The total extent is 35 elements, so 27 is valid. Dividing by the number of rows instead would invert a column-major representation. Address 4313 would be inside this element but not its start, so it would fail the element-start divisibility check.

Question 5. Recover a missing column extent

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

In row-major storage of four-byte elements, A[1,2] starts at 1028 and A[3,1] starts at 1064. Both dimensions start at zero. Determine the number of columns, then the base address.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Subtract the addresses to eliminate the base. The offset difference is 2C-1 elements, so 4(2C-1)=36 and C=5. Substitute the first observation: 1028=B+4(5+2), giving B=1000. A necessary consistency check is that columns 1 and 2 fit within five columns; at least four rows must exist because row 3 is present. The pair of observations does not determine the total row count. An answer that reports a unique complete matrix shape goes beyond the evidence.

Question 6. Distinguish row-major from column-major numerically

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A 4×6 matrix begins at 800, uses two-byte elements and zero-based indices. Calculate the address of (2,3) in each layout and explain why the addresses need not differ at every index.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Row-major offset is 2·6+3=15, yielding 830. Column-major offset is 3·4+2=14, yielding 828. Equality of the two layouts at an index requires i(C-1)=j(R-1); here 5i=3j. Both layouts start at the same address for (0,0), and the last element also occupies their common final slot. Therefore a single matching address does not identify the layout. The two formulas describe separately declared representations, not two legal interpretations of one C rectangular-array object.

Question 7. Three-dimensional mixed-radix recovery

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A row-major array has extents 3×4×5, base 2000 and four-byte elements. Find the address of (2,1,3), then recover the indices of element offset 47.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The selected offset is (2·4+1)5+3=48, giving address 2192. To invert 47, first divide by five: final index 2 and quotient 9. Divide 9 by four: middle index 1 and first index 2. Thus 47 belongs to (2,1,2), the immediate predecessor in the final axis. There are 60 elements, so both offsets are valid. A common error sums the three indices without strides, which loses the complete earlier planes and rows. The product-of-extents bound is a separate part of the inverse proof.

Question 8. A transpose changes the destination shape

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A 2×5 row-major matrix is copied into a 5×2 transpose. Where does original flat offset 7 move, and where does offset 9 move?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Divide by the original column count five: offset 7 is original (1,2). Transpose to destination (2,1), whose new row-major offset is 2·2+1=5. Offset 9 is original (1,4), which moves to (4,1), destination offset 9. A fixed last element therefore does not imply that the whole transpose is unchanged. The destination stride uses two columns, not five. The mapping iC+j↦jR+i is a bijection because transposing the recovered destination coordinates returns the original pair.

Question 9. Affine strides with a reversed axis

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A numerical view has row stride 40 bytes and column stride -4 bytes. Its logical (0,0) starts at address 1020, and its shape is 3×6. Find the addresses of (2,5) and (1,0), and the minimum and maximum selected element-start addresses.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The address map is 1020+40i-4j. At (2,5) it yields 1080; at (1,0) it yields 1060. Since the row term increases and the column term decreases, the minimum start is (0,5) at 1000 and maximum is (2,0) at 1100. This view selects rows in reverse column order and has gaps between rows. Shape alone cannot substitute the usual dense row-major formula. The numerical model still needs a backing allocation covering every selected element; its bounds are logical bounds, not a proof of C pointer provenance.

Question 10. Packed lower triangle and symmetric lookup

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A zero-based symmetric 6×6 matrix stores its lower triangle including the diagonal, in row order, with eight-byte elements and base 3000. Find the stored address for logical (1,4).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Symmetry redirects (1,4) to lower-triangle position (4,1). Four earlier rows contain 1+2+3+4=10 elements. Add column offset one to obtain flat offset 11 and address 3088. The full packed length is 6·7/2=21, not 36. Applying the lower-triangle formula directly to an upper-triangle coordinate would violate its domain and can collide with another row. This answer assumes symmetry of values and the specified storage convention; a general matrix cannot discard its upper half this way.

Question 11. Packed upper triangle cannot reuse the lower formula

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

An upper-triangular 5×5 matrix includes its diagonal and is packed by rows. Find the flat offset of (2,4), and identify which coordinates occupy flat offset 9.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Earlier row lengths are five and four, totaling nine. Within row two, column four is two positions after its first column two, so the offset is 11. Offset 9 is the beginning of row two and therefore belongs to (2,2). The general preceding-row count is in-i(i-1)/2; adding j-i yields the required offset. Row lengths decrease here, whereas they increase in lower-triangle storage. Both representations have 15 elements, but equal total capacity is not enough to identify their individual element positions.

Question 12. Repeated jagged boundaries

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Rows have lengths [2,0,3,1]. Construct the packed boundary array and recover the logical coordinate for flat offsets 2 and 5.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Prefix accumulation gives Q=[0,2,2,5,6]. Offset 2 lies in row two, interval [2,5), at column zero; the empty row one also begins at boundary two but contains no element. Offset 5 lies in row three, interval [5,6), at column zero. Taking the first equal boundary would wrongly choose the empty row for offset 2. The valid reconstruction finds i with Q[i]≤o<Q[i+1]. The final boundary 6 is one-past and has no coordinate. Every valid flat offset is covered by exactly one nonempty interval.

Question 13. Diagonal offsets and loop count

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For an n×n dense row-major matrix, derive the diagonal offsets and their sum, then evaluate for n=5. Count distinct positions selected.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Coordinate (i,i) has flat offset in+i=i(n+1) for i=0 through n-1. Their sum is (n+1)n(n-1)/2. At n=5 the offsets are 0,6,12,18,24 and the sum is 60. There are five positions, not 25; the arithmetic progression spacing is n+1. For n=0 the abstract selected set and sum are empty, while a C fixed zero-size declaration is a separate invalid construction. The sum of offsets does not equal the sum of matrix values unless values were specifically defined from their offsets.

Question 14. When is a flat byte difference meaningful?

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Two separate malloc allocations appear at numerical addresses 1000 and 1040 on one run. Each stores integers. Is their C pointer difference necessarily ten? Explain what additional facts are needed.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

No portable pointer-difference result follows. C subtraction requires both pointers to be within the same array object or its one-past boundary, with a representable ptrdiff_t result. Separate allocations fail that object relation even if they are adjacent numerically. Four-byte integers and the observed difference forty support only a numerical address calculation under that run’s representation. They do not create a shared array. If instead both pointers designate positions zero and ten of one live integer array, with legal endpoints and representable subtraction, the result is ten elements.

Question 15. Interior negative indexing is ordinary pointer arithmetic

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For int a[7]={2,4,6,8,10,12,14}, let p=a+4. Evaluate p[-3], p[2], and the complete range of legal element-access offsets k.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

p designates a[4]. Subtracting three selects a[1], so p[-3]=4; adding two selects a[6], so p[2]=14. Element access requires 0≤4+k<7, hence -4≤k≤2. Offset three forms the legal one-past pointer p+3 but cannot be dereferenced. This negative index is relative to the pointer’s current position, not Python’s end-of-sequence normalization. The legality follows from the shared live array object and bounds, rather than from the sign of the written subscript.

Question 16. Array sizeof and parameter sizeof

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Assume sizeof(int)=4 and sizeof(int *)=8. For a real int a[9], evaluate sizeof a / sizeof a[0]. What does the same expression mean inside void f(int a[9])?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

In the caller’s actual-array scope, sizeof a is 36 and sizeof a[0] is four, so the quotient is nine. In f, the array-parameter declaration is adjusted to int *, even though nine appears in its syntax. sizeof a is therefore eight and the quotient is two; it is not a runtime length computation. The length must be passed or supplied by a valid interface contract. Different pointer sizes would change the misleading quotient, while the true caller array length would remain nine. No array elements are read by these non-VLA sizeof expressions.

Question 17. Whole-array pointer versus first-element pointer

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For int a[6] and sizeof(int)=4, compare the numerical advances of a+1 and &a+1. Why can both begin at the same storage?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

After expression conversion, a+1 has type int * and advances to the next integer, numerically four bytes in the given model. &a is a pointer to the whole six-int array, so &a+1 advances over 24 bytes to one past that entire array object. Their beginnings coincide because the first element starts at the array beginning. The identical beginning does not make their pointed-to types or strides identical. The whole-array one-past result is valid to form, but dereferencing it would ask for a nonexistent following array object.

Question 18. A row pointer retains the inner extent

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For int m[3][5] with four-byte integers, let p=m. Interpret p+2, *(p+2), and sizeof *(p+2). Is p correctly declared int **?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The converted type is pointer to a five-int row: int (*p)[5]. Adding two advances two complete rows, forty bytes, to row two. Dereferencing gives the row-array lvalue m[2]; in ordinary expressions it can then convert to an int * to that row’s first element. sizeof on this row-array operand is 20. Declaring p as int ** would falsely expect stored pointer objects where integers are actually stored. A cast cannot repair that representation mismatch. Both the row index and any subsequent column index need their own valid bounds.

Question 19. Numerical adjacency does not erase a C subarray boundary

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For int m[2][3], does a int *p=m[0] authorize p[4] merely because the matrix stores six adjacent integers?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

No portable justification follows from total adjacency. p points into the first three-element row subarray. Its permitted pointer formation reaches that row’s one-past boundary, but p[4] goes beyond it. Use m[1][1], whose row and column accesses are each within their proper array objects, to select the physically corresponding integer. A separately allocated genuine six-int flat buffer would allow flat[4]. The row-major numerical offset four is useful for deriving layout; it is not a replacement for the typed object-boundary requirements of C pointer arithmetic.

Question 20. Partial initialization and definite values

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

At block scope consider int a[5]={9,2}; int b[5]; static int c[5]; Which values of a[4], b[4], c[4] are determined by these declarations?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The initializer for a supplies two entries and zero-initializes the remaining three, so a[4]=0. c has static storage duration and no explicit initializer, which also zero-initializes all its integer elements, so c[4]=0. b is an uninitialized automatic array; b[4] cannot be assigned a portable numeric output by reading it. This is not an array-bound error—index four fits—but an initialization problem. Correct tracing separates valid storage, valid index and a usable stored value. Changing the scope or initialization of b can change that third condition.

Question 21. Constraint violation is not a surprise numeric output

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Which declarations or statements require a C diagnostic: int a[3]; int b[3]; a=b; int z[0];? How do you copy the contents instead?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Array assignment a=b violates a constraint because an array object is not a modifiable lvalue for assignment. A fixed array bound zero also violates the array-declaration requirements; accepting it as an extension does not make it standard C. Declare valid arrays and copy elements in a bounded loop, or use an appropriate nonoverlapping byte-copy operation for suitable objects. An array name does not become a writable pointer variable merely because it often converts to a pointer in expressions. Rebinding a separate pointer changes the reference, not the original array contents.

Question 22. One-past use and dereference are different questions

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For a four-element initialized array, classify a+4, *(a+4), a+5 and (a+4)-a under C17.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

a+4 forms the permitted one-past pointer. Dereferencing it to read or write an element is invalid because there is no fifth element. a+5 exceeds even the permitted one-past boundary and is invalid pointer arithmetic. Subtracting a from a+4 is permitted within the same array relation and returns four elements if that result fits ptrdiff_t. The pointer’s permitted formation and the object’s permitted access are distinct checks. The legal subtraction does not require a read at the endpoint, and it does not make the endpoint into a real element.

Question 23. Unsigned reverse loop trap

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Explain why for(size_t i=n-1; i>=0; --i) use(a[i]); is incorrect. Give a version that also handles n=0 and prove its first and last accessed indices.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The condition i>=0 is always true for unsigned size_t. At n=0, n-1 wraps before any valid index exists; at nonzero n, decrementing zero wraps to a huge value instead of stopping. Initialize i=n, test i>0, decrement i, then access a[i]. For n>0 the first body decrements to n-1. Each subsequent body selects one smaller index; the final access is zero, after which the next test fails. For n=0 the body is skipped. This proves n valid accesses and avoids relying on unsigned wraparound as termination.

Question 24. A stride count with nonzero boundaries

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A loop visits indices 3,7,11,... while i<26. List the final index and number of visits; derive the count without simulating every iteration.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Write i=3+4t. The guard becomes 3+4t<26, so 0≤t≤5. There are six visits and the last index is 23. Equivalently the count is ⌈(26-3)/4⌉=6. Replacing the strict guard by i<=26 happens to give the same result here because 26 is not in the progression; that coincidence is not a general equivalence. At boundary 27 the strict and non-strict guards would differ. An array hosting the loop must contain every selected index, not merely the number of visits.

Question 25. Two different reduction initializations

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For [5,5,2,2,7,1,1], compare the number of comparisons and successful minimum updates when initialized from the first element versus mathematical positive infinity, always using strict comparison.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Initializing from the first element leaves six later comparisons. Strict decreases occur at value two and value one, so there are two updates. Initializing from infinity performs seven comparisons and the first five is an additional update, giving three. Equal occurrences never update under strict comparison, so the selected minimum position is the first one, index five. A non-strict comparison changes tie handling and update count. The number of loop comparisons is fixed here, whereas successful assignments depend on the data and initialization policy.

Question 26. Weighted prefix invariant

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For mathematical integers A=[2,-1,4,3], compute S=sum((i+1)A[i]) and give a loop invariant for the weighted scan.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The contributions are 2,-2,12,12, so S=24. At boundary i the invariant is 0≤i≤4 and

S=∑k=0i-1(k+1)A[k]

. It starts with the empty sum zero. When i<4, reading A[i] is valid and adding (i+1)A[i] extends the relation through that index. Advancing i preserves the boundary condition. At exit i=4 and the invariant gives the required result. A loop that uses i rather than i+1 computes a different weighting, so an unweighted total cannot serve as its certificate.

Question 27. Prefix construction and three ranges

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Construct P for A=[3,-2,5,1,-4]. Find sums on [1:4), [0:5) and [3:3).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Start P[0]=0 and accumulate each original element to obtain P=[0,3,1,6,7,3]. The first sum is P[4]-P[1]=7-3=4. The whole-array sum is P[5]-P[0]=3. The empty range subtracts P[3] from itself and is zero. P has six entries for five data elements because its indices label boundaries. Using P[r-1]-P[l] would omit the final included element and fail for empty ranges. After changing any data entry, update the affected prefixes before reusing these answers.

Question 28. Difference-array range updates

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Starting from five zeros, add 4 on [1:4), then subtract 2 on [2:5). Use a six-entry boundary difference array and reconstruct the result.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The first update adds four at boundary one and subtracts four at boundary four. The second subtracts two at boundary two and adds two at boundary five. D becomes [0,4,-2,0,-4,2]. Accumulating its first five entries gives [0,4,2,2,-2]. The sixth entry is a sentinel that brings the running total back to zero beyond the array; it is not a sixth data value. The signs follow from starting and ending each added constant segment. Applying both plus signs at the right boundaries would continue the change after the intended interval.

Question 29. Rectangle inclusion–exclusion

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For A=[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], build the boundary prefix table and find the sum of rows [0:2), columns [1:3).

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Include a zero row and column to obtain P=[[0,0,0,0],[0,1,3,6],[0,5,12,21]]. The requested sum is

P[2,3]-P[0,3]-P[2,1]+P[0,1]=21-0-5+0=16

. Directly, the selected entries are 2,3,5,6, also totaling 16. The table recurrence removes the overlap already counted by the top and left accumulated rectangles. Boundary indexing avoids substituting -1 at the top edge. The same four-term relation yields zero for an empty row or column interval.

Question 30. An in-place recurrence uses modified predecessors

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For A=[1,2,3,4,5], execute A[i]+=A[i-1] for i=1..4 in increasing order. Derive the general final relation to original values.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The successive complete states are [1,3,3,4,5], [1,3,6,4,5], [1,3,6,10,5], and [1,3,6,10,15]. After processing index i, A[i] equals the sum of original entries zero through i. The already updated predecessor supplies the earlier prefix, so the operation implements a prefix accumulation. A formula A0[i]+A0[i-1] would incorrectly assume an untouched predecessor. This can be proved by induction on i: the base leaves A[0] original, and each update adds the next original value to the established prefix.

Question 31. Reverse execution computes another map

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Execute the same update A[i]+=A[i-1] on [1,2,3,4,5] for i=4,3,2,1. Why is the result not a prefix sum?

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The reverse order yields [1,2,3,4,9], then [1,2,3,7,9], then [1,2,5,7,9], and finally [1,3,5,7,9]. At each update the predecessor index is lower and has not yet been changed. Therefore the final value for i>0 is A0[i]+A0[i-1], not a growing prefix total. Index zero remains original. Both executions use valid indices and the same statement, so the difference is a data dependency rather than an undefined-behavior issue. A snapshot-based implementation would make the neighbor-sum intent explicit.

Question 32. An overlapping right move fails in forward order

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

For original A=[2,4,6,8,10,12], copy four entries from source offset 0 to destination offset 1, in increasing t. Give all resulting writes and compare with an original-value move.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

At t=0, A[1] receives 2. At t=1, the source A[1] has already become 2, so A[2] also receives 2. The same dependency propagates through t=2 and t=3. The final array is [2,2,2,2,2,12]. The desired snapshot move is [2,2,4,6,8,12]. All individual indices are valid; the failure is preservation of unread original values. Copying the same region in descending t avoids it, because each source is read before a higher destination overwrites it.

Question 33. An overlapping right move succeeds in reverse order

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Repeat the previous move but process t=3,2,1,0. State the unchanged region and a suffix invariant.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Writes occur as A[4]=A[3]=8, A[3]=A[2]=6, A[2]=A[1]=4, and A[1]=A[0]=2. The final array is [2,2,4,6,8,12], while positions zero and five remain unchanged. Before a descending step t, every destination d+k for k>t contains original source s+k, and the remaining source prefix through s+t is unchanged. Since d>s, writing d+t cannot affect any still unread smaller source position. The invariant proves both the final destination and absence of damage outside the moved region.

Question 34. Leftward overlap needs the opposite direction

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

Move four entries of [2,4,6,8,10,12] from source offset 1 to destination offset 0. Compare increasing and decreasing processing orders.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Increasing order writes values 4,6,8,10 into positions zero through three, giving [4,6,8,10,10,12]. Each destination is below the current source, so no future larger source index is overwritten. Decreasing order first writes A[3]=10; the next read of A[3] therefore repeats ten, eventually producing [10,10,10,10,10,12]. This reverses the safety relation of a rightward move. The correct rule depends on relative offsets and overlap, not on a universal preference for increasing or decreasing loops.

Question 35. Bounds alone do not prove a copy contract

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Course-inspired extension — CMU 15-122 Lecture 3, exercise 2

A copy_into loop has valid source/destination bounds but its postcondition compares final source and final destination segments. Explain why those bounds are insufficient if both parameters alias.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Take a=[1,2,3,4], source start zero, target start one and length three. A forward loop produces [1,1,1,1]. Its final source segment and target segment happen to be equal, yet the intended original-value copy [1,1,2,3] was not achieved. In the opposite direction, a forward move produces [2,3,4,4] and even final source/target equality can fail. Therefore a meaningful specification must refer to original source values and control interference. Require disjointness, or use a snapshot/overlap-safe move. The CMU array-copy exercise is extended here precisely to expose this missing obligation.

Question 36. Copy a segment with a complete proof

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Course-inspired extension — CMU 15-122 Lecture 3, exercise 1

For initialized A of length n and 0≤l≤r≤n, construct a distinct B of length r-l with B[k]=original A[l+k]. State initialization, preservation, exit and termination.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Initialize t=0 and use the invariant 0≤t≤r-l plus equality for all copied positions k<t. Initially the equality is vacuous. When t<r-l, destination t is valid and source l+t satisfies l≤l+t<r≤n. Writing that original source extends the equality through k=t; distinct storage ensures that the source is unchanged. Advance t to preserve the bound. At exit t=r-l and every result position satisfies the contract. The nonnegative variant r-l-t decreases each time. When l=r, allocate/represent a distinct empty result appropriately without a zero-size fixed C declaration.

Question 37. Insertion shifts and the end case

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

A logical sequence [3,6,9,12] occupies the first four positions of capacity six. Insert 7 at index two. Give the write order, new contents and shift count; compare insertion at index four.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Move original index three to four, then index two to three, then write seven at index two. The logical result is [3,6,7,9,12], length five. There are n-k=2 shifts; descending movement preserves the original values. Insertion at boundary four uses zero shifts and writes only the new last value. Boundary n is valid for insertion although it is not a valid old element index. Capacity must permit the new length, and spare positions need not have meaningful initialized values before they are assigned.

Question 38. Deletion changes length rather than erasing storage

The physical slot at old index four can still contain fifteen; it is outside the logical sequence and need not be zeroed for correctness. Reading it as an allocated initialized element is a different question from including it in the container’s valid logical contents. Question 42. A stable read/write filter

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Remove odd entries from [5,2,7,4,6,9,8] in place without changing the order of retained entries. Give final logical contents and explain why writes cannot destroy unread data.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Use read r from zero upward and write w starting at zero. Copy a[r] to a[w] only when the entry is even, then increment w. Retained entries are 2,4,6,8, giving logical length four and prefix [2,4,6,8]. At every boundary 0≤w≤r≤7, and the output prefix equals the retained original entries from the processed prefix. Because w≤r, a retained write affects the current or an earlier position, never a larger unread position. Stability follows because retained values are appended in original encounter order.

Question 43. Dependency analysis of a two-pass difference transform

Process from index three down to one. The writes are 10-9=1, then 9-5=4, then 5-3=2, so the final sequence is [3,2,4,1]. Each predecessor is still original when read. Question 44. Python single indices and clipped slices

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

The single index -2 normalizes to four and returns 4. For the second expression, start -8 clips to zero and stop 20 clips to six; step three selects indices zero and three, giving [0,3]. Question 47. Ordinary slice assignment can change length

Question 48. Outer copy and inner alias

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Course-inspired extension — UC Berkeley CS61A, Composing Programs §2.4.2

b[0].append(7)
b[1] = [9]

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Question 49. Repeated rows share one inner object

Question 50. Deletion during iteration skips shifted entries

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The iterator first selects two at position zero and removes it, leaving [4,6,7]. Its next index is one, which now contains six rather than four, so it removes six and leaves [4,7]. The next index is two, beyond the current list, and iteration ends. Final result is [4,7], despite four also being even. Question 51. Identity versus equal contents

Initially a==b is true because the contents compare equal, but a is b is false because the outer slice made a different list. a[0] is b[0] is true because the shallow copy retained its inner references. a[0] is c[0] is false because the row slicing created distinct inner lists. Question 55. An exactly filled C character array lacks a terminator

Question 56. Writable array versus literal target

Question 57. Bounded length finds a terminator or reports absence

Question 58. Naive matching comparison count

Question 64. Exact doubling work for a particular length

Question 65. General doubling bound and exact powers

Each expansion copies its previous full capacity, so the sum is 1+2+…+c/2=c-1. At c=1 no expansion occurs and the empty sum is zero, matching the formula. Choosing the least power of two at least n gives n≤c<2n, hence c-1<2n. Including new writes gives less than 3n. If n itself is a power of two, c=n and the exact copy work is n-1. Question 69. A failed realloc must not lose the owner

Each deletion reaches length four and copies four elements into a capacity-four block. The next append finds that block full, copies four elements into capacity eight and writes the new item. Question 72. A precise cold cache-line comparison

One cache line holds eight integers, exactly one row. Row-major traversal reads all eight entries of a row after one fill and then moves to the next line, totaling eight fills. The read occupies bytes from relative offset eight through 8+44-1=51. Line indices range from floor(8/16)=0 through floor(51/16)=3, so four distinct lines are touched. Dividing the total 44 bytes by sixteen and rounding up gives three, but misses the partially occupied initial and final lines due to alignment. The exact interval formula is

⌊(B+nw-1)/L⌋-⌊B/L⌋+1

for positive n. A zero-length read touches no lines and must be handled before subtracting one.
